title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Food & Agriculture
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

items.title: France expects EU sanctions on 14 December over Iran’s sabotage of supermarket refrigeration, as Iran-linked hackers turn to physical attacks
items.content_text: France’s foreign minister said on 17 November he expects EU foreign ministers to agree sanctions on 14 December against those behind October’s sabotage of supermarket refrigeration controllers, a day after EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas confirmed new Iran sanctions are being prepared. Paris blames the IRGC’s Shahid Kaveh unit for the attack on about 700 French sites, which French authorities say caused at least 15 fires, and has sought arrest warrants for three officers; Iran rejects the accusations. Health-ISAC warned on 16 November that settings were also changed at French blood-service sites. US and Israeli officials told the Wall Street Journal that Iran-linked hackers also sabotaged equipment at small Midwest water stations and aboard two tankers. For grocers, cold stores and food processors, a state-backed actor has shown it will spoil food stock by remote control (editorial assessment).

items.title: CISA and FBI warn of an ongoing threat to internet-connected refrigeration as European supermarket attacks reach at least 11 countries
items.content_text: On 5 November CISA and the FBI, with HHS, USDA and DOT, warned that hackers tampering with internet-connected refrigeration controllers pose an ongoing threat that also reaches cold-storage, healthcare, chemical and transport operations. After hundreds of French stores were hit in October, a second wave on 1–2 November reached about 11 European countries, forcing units into continuous heating or defrost. Sweden’s NCSC says Coop and ICA victims mainly ran older systems from one manufacturer with weak passwords. Belgium’s interior minister said on 12 November that evidence points to Iran, short of formal attribution; a pro-Russian claim is unverified. Exposed Danfoss StoreView instances fell from 3,004 to 708 by 5 November, and Sekoia says the second wave used a non-public flaw that renames the controller’s admin account. Any reachable controller is at risk today (editorial assessment).

items.title: A security breach keeps USDA payment, loan and mapping systems offline for farmers for most of a week
items.content_text: The US Department of Agriculture has kept many applications offline since about 16 November after its security operations centre found an intrusion, including payment, loan and mapping tools that farmers and field staff use. An internal email reported by Nextgov says IT staff reset every database password across all environments, which caused the outages. On 20 November Under Secretary Richard Fordyce called it a cyberthreat, said no personal information was involved and no data was lost, and expected most systems back within days. Former officials quoted by NBC News say data theft has not been ruled out. No attacker has been named and nothing points to OT. Food and agriculture operators should plan for agency systems they depend on being unavailable for a week (editorial assessment).

items.title: The Pentagon still will not say whether August commissary freezer failures were a cyberattack, as Army investigators work with French police
items.content_text: Investigators are still treating late-August refrigeration failures at no fewer than six US military commissaries, the on-base grocery stores, as a suspected cyberattack, with no cause confirmed. Reuters reported on 29 October, citing unnamed officials, that refrigerators and freezers switched to defrost and warmed, spoiling food at bases including Fort Huachuca and Fort Irwin, and that US Cyber Command has joined Army and Air Force inquiries. Stars and Stripes reported on 4 November that the Army CID cyber field office is working with the Defense Criminal Investigative Service and with French law enforcement on the October attacks in France; the Pentagon still declines to say whether a cyberattack occurred or how many stores were hit. Nextgov/FCW sources suspect Iran-linked hackers; no agency has attributed it. The forced-defrost pattern matches France, but this remains unconfirmed (editorial assessment).

items.title: Attackers rooted unpatched Check Point gateways through PHP2Shell, planted backdoors and wiped a VMware host; the root flaw is now in KEV
items.content_text: Check Point Research said on 12 November that attackers exploited the PHP2Shell flaws on unpatched Check Point Mobile Access portals from 30 October, then used a local flaw (CVE-2026-123039) to become root. They planted backdoors, pivoted to a VMware ESXi host and ran a wiper. The first wave hit Israeli organizations, some destructively; a second wave from 2 November reached several countries without destruction. Attribution is unconfirmed (tooling resembles China-nexus UNC5221). CISA added the root flaw to KEV on 13 November. No OT victim is reported, but these firewalls often sit at the IT/OT boundary and ESXi often hosts HMIs and historians (editorial assessment).

items.title: Cyberattack on Brazil’s Santos port authority forces manual workarounds at Latin America’s busiest port
items.content_text: The Port of Santos authority, which runs Brazil’s largest port, lost its IT systems on 6 November and on 10 November confirmed a cyberattack. Access-control systems and digital tools for coordinating port operations went down, delaying vessel, truck and train procedures and forcing some checks, such as matching ship dimensions to berths, to be done by hand. The port’s protection level was raised to 2 of 3 on 8 November. By 16 November main internal systems were in final tests and about 70% of affected file backups were recovered; ship movements and landside access continued throughout. Brazil’s Federal Police are investigating; the attacker, entry route and any data theft are undisclosed. Santos is a major outlet for Brazilian agricultural exports such as sugar, soy and coffee, so food and ag shippers should confirm their forwarders’ manual fallbacks (editorial assessment).

items.title: PHP2Shell attacks rooted about two dozen Palo Alto firewalls, and Siemens, Schneider and ABB now list grid-control, DCS and RTU products, several with no fix
items.content_text: Palo Alto’s Unit 42 verified that a suspected China-nexus actor chained the PHP2Shell flaws (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) with Linux kernel bug CVE-2026-46300 to root about two dozen internet-exposed PAN-OS firewalls on 23–24 October and steal Active Directory credentials. Siemens (Spectrum Power, AMIS TS and, since 16 November, WTV676/WTV776 metering gateways), Schneider (a Foxboro DCS server) and ABB (Netcontrol RTUs, ASPECT gateways) now list affected products, several unfixed. None is reported exploited and no OT operator is named: treat it as an IT-to-OT boundary warning.

items.title: Dragos counts 1,266 ransomware attacks on industrial organizations in Q3, up 11%, and found no case of an operator touching a control system
items.content_text: Dragos said on 16 November that ransomware hit 1,266 industrial organizations between July and September 2026, up 11% on the second quarter, while the number of brands claiming industrial victims rose from 70 to 99. Manufacturing took 69% of cases, followed by the ICS ecosystem of integrators and equipment makers (116) and transport and logistics (105). Qilin and The Gentlemen drove 29% of the total. Dragos saw no Q3 case of an operator manipulating a control system: production stopped because the IT, ERP and virtualization layers plants rely on went down, as when dairy maker Fairlife reportedly halted all four of its US plants for about 11 days. Entry came through edge devices and enterprise applications exploited within days of disclosure, and through stolen VPN and firewall credentials.

items.title: DHS tells Congress Iran-backed hackers have stepped up attacks on US water, energy and transport since February, while officials rule out hacking in last week’s outages
items.content_text: In written testimony for a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on 18 November, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Iranian state-sponsored groups and pro-Iranian criminals have targeted US critical infrastructure since the conflict with Iran began in February, increasingly in transportation, healthcare, water, energy and financial services. He described most attacks so far as localized, low-damage disruptions of poorly secured industrial control systems, but warned that weak cyber hygiene could have devastating consequences. At the same hearing, officials said they found no evidence that hackers caused recent outages such as the FAA ground stop. AttackIQ research released on 17 November describes Iranian groups handing network access to one another, often reaching targets through contractors and suppliers. For food operators, the US view now matches France’s: Iran goes after the weakest exposed controllers (editorial assessment).

items.title: UK NCSC: AI-assisted attacks are exploiting familiar weaknesses in internet-facing services faster than defenders can react
items.content_text: The UK National Cyber Security Centre said on 24 November that since September it has seen a rise in AI-assisted, “agentic” attacks, in which automated tooling finds and exploits well-known weaknesses in internet-facing services at speed. The weaknesses are not new: exposed management interfaces, default or reused passwords, and unpatched edge devices. What has changed is how quickly they are found and used. The NCSC’s advice is to shrink the internet-facing footprint, patch exposed systems first and remove services that do not need to be reachable. That is the same exposure the refrigeration attackers used at European supermarkets, so grocers, cold stores and processors should expect web-managed controllers to be found within hours of going online (editorial assessment).

items.title: Switzerland confirms its first AI-agent cyberattacks on critical infrastructure, using the same weak passwords and exposed systems behind the refrigeration attacks
items.content_text: Switzerland’s Federal Office for Cybersecurity (BACS) said on 26 November that five recent attacks used AI agents, frameworks that find weaknesses, pick tools and plan their next steps largely on their own. Four of the five compromised systems, and three targets were critical-infrastructure operators, which public broadcaster SRF identified as electricity, water and telecommunications providers. BACS named no victims or attacker and has not said whether any control systems were reached. The entry points were ordinary: default or easily guessed passwords and known flaws in internet-facing systems, the pattern the UK NCSC described on 24 November. No food company is named, but these are the weaknesses behind the supermarket refrigeration attacks, so exposed controllers and remote-access portals will be found faster than before (editorial assessment).

items.title: Claroty finds 65,000 game consoles, smart speakers and cars on critical-infrastructure networks, most of them on production segments
items.content_text: Claroty said on 17 November that, across 45 million devices at more than 30,000 critical-infrastructure sites, it found about 65,000 consumer gadgets that do not belong on operational networks: game consoles, smart-home and entertainment devices, and connected cars. Industrial sites held 963 game consoles, nearly 90% of them on production rather than guest networks, and thousands of connected vehicles were attached to site networks with almost none isolated on a guest segment. The study does not break out food plants, but processing sites, cold stores and farms with shared Wi-Fi face the same problem. Each unmanaged device is a foothold that quietly undermines the segmentation protecting packaging lines and refrigeration controls (editorial assessment).

items.title: Hackers probe 14 newly disclosed flaws in end-of-life Copeland XWEB EVO refrigeration controllers, five of which will never be fixed
items.content_text: VulnCheck has disclosed 14 vulnerabilities in Copeland’s XWEB EVO, the Dixell supervisor that runs supermarket and cold-storage refrigeration. Firmware built before a 2021 rewrite is open to unauthenticated configuration writes (CVE-2026-124014) and unauthenticated root command execution (CVE-2026-124010). Five flaws reach the latest firmware: four predictable admin credentials derived from the device’s MAC address and the date, and one authenticated command injection. Copeland ended XWEB EVO support on 16 March 2026, will not fix them and advises moving to XWEB Pro. VulnCheck saw probing within about two hours of the 12 November CVE publication, from opportunistic scanners rather than the October campaign. Onyphe counts about 2,000 internet-exposed XWEB EVO hosts against 108 XWEB Pro, and CERT-FR named XWEB among the controllers hit in France. Every exposed unit is a standing risk (editorial assessment).

items.title: CISA rates the Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA refrigeration-manager flaw CVSS 9.8, with no fixed version yet; Danfoss says the fix comes in 5.5.x
items.content_text: CISA published advisory ICSA-26-328-03 on 24 November for Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA system managers, the store-level controllers that run supermarket and cold-storage refrigeration. CVE-2026-129713 (CVSS v3.1 9.8) is a stack-based buffer overflow in an unauthenticated web handler: a crafted HTTP or HTTPS POST corrupts memory and restarts the web server, and code execution is possible but not demonstrated. Software 5.4.0 and earlier is affected, settling the earlier dispute over whether 5.4.0 was safe. CISA names no fixed version; Danfoss says the fix comes in 5.5.x. Danfoss’s 20 November advisories also cover CVE-2026-127057 (CVSS v4 9.9), default credentials in legacy AK-SC 355 and AK-SM 800 units. Neither flaw is reported exploited, and the European sabotage has not been linked to them. Until 5.5.x ships, keeping these units off the internet is the real control.

items.title: A Brotli flaw already in CISA’s exploited list reaches Siemens BRAUMAT brewery batch control and WinCC; most products have no fix yet
items.content_text: Siemens says CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the widely used Brotli decoder, reaches several of its industrial software lines, and CISA republished the assessment as ICSA-26-321-03 on 17 November. The bug can crash the software, leak information or possibly allow code execution. CISA added the CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 27 October because of attacks elsewhere; nobody has reported exploitation through a Siemens product. Affected products include BRAUMAT and SISTAR V8.2, WinCC OA V3.20 and V3.21, WinCC Runtime Professional, WinCC V7/V8 and TIA Administrator. Fixes exist only for BRAUMAT/SISTAR (V8.2 Update 5) and WinCC OA V3.20 (P17.1). BRAUMAT is Siemens’ process control system for breweries and beverage plants and WinCC is a common HMI on food lines, so this is the Siemens advisory most relevant to processors (editorial assessment).

items.title: A vCenter authentication bypass was exploited as a zero-day for two months before Broadcom’s 19 November patch; vCenter 7.0 gets no fix
items.content_text: Broadcom patched CVE-2026-123890 on 19 November, a critical flaw in vCenter’s directory service that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker obtain an administrator session. Google’s Mandiant, which reported the bug, says a suspected China-linked espionage group it tracks as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) exploited it for more than two months beforehand. In the incidents Mandiant investigated, the group got in through a BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw, attacked vCenter in early September with a custom tool called Bonesaw, stole SAML signing material and the vCenter master key, forged tokens and moved on to ESXi hosts. Fixes are in vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m; end-of-life vCenter 7.0 has no public patch. No victims are named. Many plants run HMIs, historians and engineering workstations as virtual machines, so whoever controls vCenter controls those hosts (editorial assessment).

items.title: Attackers root clustered Cisco Expressway gateways soon after a public exploit, and CISA adds the flaw to KEV
items.content_text: Security firm F6 says attackers exploited CVE-2026-76466, a critical flaw in clustered Cisco Expressway Core and Edge deployments, shortly after proof-of-concept code appeared on GitHub. They broke into two internet-facing Expressway nodes at an unnamed Russian organization, moved to two more cluster nodes inside the network, and gained root. From there they ran Python scripts, which F6 says show signs of AI-assisted writing, to scan for SMB shares, SQL Server and WinRM hosts and to search GitLab for credentials. CISA added the flaw to its KEV catalog on 20 November alongside the vCenter zero-day. Cisco disclosed and fixed it on 21 October; there is no workaround. No OT victim is reported, but Expressway is a perimeter gateway that often bridges outside callers into internal networks, so an exposed, unpatched cluster is a foothold close to plant-side systems (editorial assessment).

items.title: N-able ships Hotfix 3 for 17 more N-central flaws after attackers planted miners on servers already running Hotfix 2
items.content_text: N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 on 16 November as a critical security update. It fixes 17 new CVEs, including authentication bypasses, path traversal leading to code execution and a syslog injection that runs commands as root, and removes the Legacy API option that the actively exploited 4EverAble2Shell chain depends on. On-premises servers need the upgrade now, and every customer must also upgrade Agents and Probes, which N-able warns can otherwise be impersonated. The fix follows Huntback’s 13 November finding of cryptocurrency miners on 21 N-central servers. Separately, on 20 November N-able disclosed a breach of its hosted Mail Assure and SpamExperts cloud, which it says is unrelated to N-central and reached no customer data. Many integrators manage plant-side Windows hosts through RMM tools, and a miner today can be a hands-on intruder tomorrow (editorial assessment).

items.title: Java4Shell exploitation attempts begin, and Siemens tells customers to take Industrial Edge Management offline until patched
items.content_text: Probing for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption bug in how OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later decode Base64 data, started within two days of its 17 November disclosure. GreyNoise counted more than 150 matching requests from five addresses by early 19 November and Previdian logged nine attempts from six addresses; none is confirmed to have succeeded. Exploitation needs a recent Intel or AMD x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI, and researchers at Calif showed unauthenticated code execution against default Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Keycloak setups, each with a tailored chain. For OT teams the key item is Siemens advisory SSA-272816: three Industrial Edge Management products are affected, fixes are in progress, and Siemens recommends taking those instances offline until they are patched. Cisco lists more than a dozen products with no fix yet, and Atlassian Data Center products are also unpatched.

items.title: Bluetooth flaws let a nearby attacker apply or release trailer brakes on Elecbrakes controllers, and the oldest model is still unpatched
items.content_text: Element Digital researchers found three Bluetooth flaws in Elecbrakes trailer brake controllers (EB2, VM1 and ELBC 2000), two rated critical, covering missing authentication and weak replay protection. An attacker within about 100 metres could engage or release a trailer’s brakes, or change braking force, without the driver doing anything. A third, medium-severity firmware-update flaw is considered theoretical. CISA published advisory ICSA-26-323-02 last week. Elecbrakes shipped firmware for EB2 and VM1 in early July and says about 60–70% of controllers in daily use have it; a fix for the older ELBC 2000 is still in progress. There is no evidence of malicious exploitation. For farms and haulers towing livestock, grain or equipment trailers, this is a road-safety issue on a wireless link, not a plant-network one (editorial assessment).

items.title: A malicious project file can run code on engineering workstations that program AutomationDirect C-More EA9 touch panels
items.content_text: CISA published an advisory on 24 November for AutomationDirect’s C-More EA9 programming software, the Windows tool used to build and load screens for C-More EA9 operator touch panels. CVE-2026-127280 (CVSS v3 7.8) is a heap-based buffer overflow: if an engineer opens a crafted project file in version 6.80 or earlier, an attacker can run code on that workstation. CISA reports no known public exploitation and lists manufacturing, energy and water as the main sectors. AutomationDirect panels and PLCs are common on smaller food and beverage lines, packaging cells and farm equipment, and the engineering laptop that programs them usually also reaches the controllers, so a poisoned project file passed by email or USB is a realistic route onto the line (editorial assessment).

items.title: GAO finds USDA and FDA fall short on cyber threat sharing and emergency exercises for the food and agriculture sector
items.content_text: GAO reported on 19 November that USDA and the FDA, the sector’s lead federal agencies, met most cyber-related requirements Congress set in the FY2021 National Defense Authorization Act but only partially met or missed five, mainly on threat-information sharing and emergency preparedness. Both agencies cited a lack of resources and staffing, and ABC News reports they have not run food-sector cyberattack response exercises since 2024. GAO made five recommendations: two to USDA’s Office of Homeland Security and three to the FDA’s Office of Coordinated Outbreak Response, covering information sharing with CISA, preparedness exercises and, for FDA, planning documents for cyber emergencies. HHS agreed; USDA disagreed with its two and asked GAO to remove or redirect them, and GAO kept them. Plan to run your own exercises (editorial assessment).
